summary: Moses warns of locusts, and Pharaoh’s servants urge release, but Pharaoh offers to let only the men go; the locusts consume what hail spared. Pharaoh asks forgiveness yet refuses again after relief, three days of darkness follow while Israel has light, and a last dispute over livestock ends with Pharaoh threatening Moses’ life if he returns.
whyItMatters: Each proposal to release only part of the community leaves Pharaoh in control of people or herds. The account joins devastating environmental effects to the continued argument over what full freedom to serve Yahweh requires.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Pharaoh’s court and Egypt’s fields and homes during locusts and darkness, with Israelite dwellings described as lit.
context.literaryForm: Two final warning-and-plague scenes before the firstborn announcement, framed by negotiation and a broken audience.

before.text: Hail has damaged crops and killed those left in the fields; Pharaoh again refused after the storm ended. Locusts are now announced against the vegetation that remains.

here.text: Officials’ alarm, restricted release offers, locust damage, and thick darkness lead to a direct threat against Moses.

after.text: The next chapter announces one more plague, the death of firstborn throughout Egypt, before instructions for the departure night.

outline.heading: Locusts foretold for later generations
outline.note: Yahweh names hardened hearts and commands the warning that surviving plants will be eaten.

outline.heading: The servants urge release; Pharaoh limits it
outline.note: Officials see Egypt’s ruin, but Pharaoh says only men may leave.

outline.heading: Locusts and a request for relief
outline.note: An east wind brings consuming locusts; prayer and a west wind remove them, yet Pharaoh refuses.

outline.heading: Three days of darkness
outline.note: Egypt cannot see or move normally, while Israelite dwellings have light.

outline.heading: Livestock dispute and a final threat
outline.note: Pharaoh allows people but not flocks; Moses refuses, and Pharaoh threatens him.

keyVerses.text: Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve Yahweh, their God. Don’t you yet know that Egypt is destroyed?”
keyVerses.why: Pharaoh’s servants themselves say Egypt is being destroyed and urge a change.

keyVerses.text: Moses said, “We will go with our young and with our old. We will go with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds; for we must hold a feast to Yahweh.”
keyVerses.why: Moses specifies that young, old, sons, daughters, and livestock are all part of the requested departure.

keyVerses.text: They didn’t see one another, and nobody rose from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.
keyVerses.why: The darkness is narrated with a contrast between Egyptian paralysis and Israelite light.

questions.question: Why do Pharaoh’s servants urge him to act?
questions.answer: They call Moses a snare and ask whether Pharaoh recognizes that Egypt is destroyed. Their appeal follows the damage of earlier plagues and precedes the locusts, showing concern within the royal administration.

questions.question: Why does Moses reject an offer for the men to go?
questions.answer: He says the feast must include young and old, sons and daughters, and their flocks and herds. Pharaoh’s offer would leave families and property behind, so it does not match the departure Moses says is required.

questions.question: What are “locusts” doing here?
questions.answer: A wind brings them in enormous numbers, and they eat the green growth and fruit that the hail left. The land is darkened by their coverage before another wind drives them away.

questions.question: Does Pharaoh’s plea for forgiveness change his decision?
questions.answer: He says he sinned and asks Moses to pray away the locusts. The insects leave after prayer, but the narrator says Yahweh hardens his heart and he still does not release Israel.

questions.question: Who experiences the three days of darkness?
questions.answer: The narrator says Egyptians cannot see one another and no one rises from his place, while Israelites have light in their dwellings. It gives duration and contrast but no physical mechanism for the darkness.

questions.question: Why does livestock remain a sticking point after the darkness?
questions.answer: Pharaoh allows children to leave but wants the flocks and herds left behind. Moses says animals are needed for sacrifice and that they do not yet know exactly what will be required, so not even a hoof can remain.

questions.question: What purpose is given for telling children and grandchildren about the signs?
questions.answer: Yahweh says Moses’ descendants should hear what was done in Egypt so that they may know he is Yahweh. The proposed memory makes the confrontation part of a continuing family account rather than an event known only to witnesses.

questions.question: How does the audience with Pharaoh end?
questions.answer: Pharaoh orders Moses away and threatens death if he sees his face again. Moses agrees he will not see Pharaoh’s face again; the chapter ends before the final announced plague occurs.
